opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic observation was that there was a big gap between how important people thought AI was going to be and how little rigorous, quantitative work existed on where it was actually heading. You had a lot of strong opinions floating around, some people saying transformative AI was decades or centuries away, others saying it was imminent, but surprisingly few people were grounding those views in data.

A lot of the questions that matter most are, at least in part, empirical. How fast is training compute growing? How much are algorithms improving, and how does that compare to hardware progress? How much data is there, and when might we run out? What does the economics of scaling look like? These are questions you can actually make progress on by carefully gathering data, building trend lines, and thinking about the underlying drivers. But in academia that kind of work doesn't fit neatly into any one discipline. It's a bit of economics, a bit of machine learning, a bit of forecasting, so it tended to fall through the cracks.

My own background was more in economics, and I'd been thinking about growth models and what happens if you can substitute compute for labor at scale. From that angle it seemed clear that AI could be an enormously consequential technology, potentially the most important economic development in a very long time. Given those stakes, it seemed crazy that there wasn't an organization dedicated to tracking the inputs and producing careful, public, well-documented estimates that policymakers, labs, and researchers could all draw on.

So the opportunity was partly being an infrastructure provider, building datasets of notable models, compute, hardware, and so on, and partly doing the analysis on top of that to sharpen people's views about timelines and impacts. We wanted the debate to be anchored in evidence rather than vibes.

r001.rationale: The candidate says this empirical work did not fit neatly into an academic discipline and tended to fall through the cracks. It does not clearly identify a mismatch with what academia can turn into publishable papers.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started Epoch, around 2022, there was this strange gap. AI was clearly becoming one of the most important technologies in the world, and yet there was almost no serious empirical work tracking it. People were having these enormous debates about timelines, about whether scaling would continue, about what compute trends looked like, and most of it was being conducted on vibes. If you wanted to know how fast training compute had grown over the past decade, or what the price-performance of GPUs was doing, or how much data the frontier labs were actually using, you basically had to go dig through dozens of papers yourself and piece it together. There was no equivalent of what economists have in, say, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, or what climate science has in its monitoring infrastructure.

So the opportunity was pretty simple in some sense. Just do the boring work. Build the datasets, collect the numbers carefully, and make them public. We thought that if you got the basic empirical foundations right, a lot of the downstream debates would become much more tractable. You could actually argue about whether compute would keep scaling at four or five times per year, rather than arguing about whether it was scaling at all.

The other piece was that I'd been doing some of this already in a more academic context. I'd worked on things like how much algorithmic progress contributes relative to hardware, and how research effort translates into output. And it was clear that these questions were not going to be answered properly within the normal incentive structure of academia, where you get a paper out and move on. You needed an institution that would maintain the data over time, update it continuously, and be accountable for being right. That's quite different from the usual research model, and it's what we tried to build.

r001.rationale: The response says important questions about AI progress and scaling would not be properly answered under academia’s incentive to publish a paper and move on, motivating an institution that maintains data over time.

astra-6.text:
The opportunity was to bring more empirical rigor to questions about where AI is going. There were a lot of strong intuitions about how quickly it might progress, but relatively little systematic work measuring the underlying trends and using those measurements to constrain forecasts.

You could look at how much compute goes into training models, how much data they use, how algorithms are improving, and how those inputs translate into capabilities. Then you could ask how long those trends can continue and what might limit them—whether that’s the availability of data, chips, or the willingness to spend more on training.

That seemed like a useful niche for an organization: building the datasets and models that let us have a more grounded discussion about AI’s future. You’re not going to predict every breakthrough, but you can make the uncertainty more precise and give people a better basis for making decisions.

r001.rationale: It describes limited systematic measurement and strong intuitions about AI progress, but does not identify a mismatch between important AI-future questions and what academia can turn into publishable papers.

sol-6.1.text:
The opportunity I saw was to make the discussion about AI’s future more empirically grounded. People had very different views about how quickly AI would advance, but there wasn’t much systematic work measuring the trends that might help us distinguish between those views.

We wanted to understand things like how the compute used to train models was growing, how much algorithms were improving, and what constraints might eventually slow that progress. Could we get enough data, chips, and investment to sustain these trends? And what would that imply for the capabilities of future systems?

The idea behind Epoch was that you could make progress on these questions by carefully collecting data and building quantitative models, even if you couldn’t predict every breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response says there was little systematic work measuring AI trends, but does not identify a mismatch between important questions about AI’s future and what academia can turn into publishable papers.
